title: Modular forms — Hecke theory, newforms, and L-functions, Part II: GL₂ automorphic representations and transfer
summary: Follow-up of the R17.5 coverage record of the R17.3 packet (which planned the stage's fifteen target nodes: quadratic induction, Tate's vanishing and projective lifting, dihedral, tetrahedral and octahedral Artin automorphy, the Langlands–Tunnell theorem, weight-one comparisons, Tunnell's globalisation, Carayol's prescribed induction and the mod-3 application). This packet closes the two source-proof gaps that record left open. First, matching at every place: Jacquet–Langlands's isolation argument (a twist with one prescribed component and high ramification at the other bad places, GL₂ stability of ε-factors, the GL₂ local converse theorem and the twisted Artin functional equation) upgrades almost-everywhere matching with a cuspidal representation to matching at every place, once the archimedean components agree; for tetrahedral and octahedral representations the archimedean components are matched through cyclic base change. Second, the reduction-compatible lift: Brauer characters, their recognition of composition factors and the Fong–Swan theorem give, for a residual representation with solvable image, a characteristic-zero lift with the same kernel whose reduction is the residual representation itself, totally odd when p > 2. With these, residual representations with solvable image are automorphic of weight one over number fields (Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni, Proposition 10.1.3) and come from weight-one newforms over Q (Dieulefait–Pacetti, Theorem 1.3).

nodes.title: Stability of GL₂ factors under highly ramified twists
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero, ψ a nontrivial additive character of F, and π an irreducible admissible representation of GL₂(F) with central character ω_π. For a quasi-character χ of F^× write c(χ) for its conductor exponent. (i) There is an integer m(π) such that L(s, χ⊗π) = L(s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃) = 1 whenever c(χ) > m(π). (ii) If π₁ and π₂ are irreducible admissible representations with the same central character, there is an integer m such that ε(s, χ⊗π₁, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π₂, ψ) whenever c(χ) > m; with (i) this gives γ(s, χ⊗π₁, ψ) = γ(s, χ⊗π₂, ψ) for such χ, where γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ)L(1−s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃)/L(s, χ⊗π). (iii) More precisely, for any factorisation ω_π = μ₁μ₂ into quasi-characters, ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) once c(χ) is large compared with c(μ₁) and c(μ₂); the right side is a product of Tate's GL₁ constants and depends on π only through ω_π. The bound m depends on π₁, π₂ and ψ, not on χ.
hypotheses: F is a finite extension of Q_p; ψ: F → C^× is a nontrivial continuous additive character.
π, π₁, π₂ are irreducible admissible representations of GL₂(F); in (ii) ω_{π₁} = ω_{π₂}.
The local factors L, ε and γ are those of Jacquet–Langlands §2–§3 (equivalently Godement–Jacquet for n = 2), in the normalisation fixed by R16.3.
c(χ) is the conductor exponent of AL.1/local-quasicharacter-conductor; 'sufficiently ramified' means c(χ) larger than an explicit bound depending on π (and on ψ through its conductor).
proofSteps: One-dimensional and principal-series representations: L(s, χ⊗π(μ₁, μ₂)) = L(s, χμ₁)L(s, χμ₂) and ε(s, χ⊗π(μ₁, μ₂), ψ) = ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) (R16.3/principal-series-parameter and the Jacquet–Langlands product formula); once c(χ) exceeds c(μ₁) and c(μ₂), both χμᵢ are ramified, so the L-factors are 1 (AL.1/ramified-local-theory) and the ε-factor is the stated product. Twists of Steinberg are constituents of a reducible principal series and have the same twisted factors as it for highly ramified χ (JL70 p. 58, reduction step).

Supercuspidal π: L(s, χ⊗π) = 1 for every χ (R16.2/local-classification and R16.3/supercuspidal-parameter). For the ε-factor, JL70 compute ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) through the Kirillov model (R16.2/supercuspidal-kirillov): for c(χ) large the Mellin transform of a vector supported near 1 only sees the central character, which yields the product ε(s, χμ₁, ψ)ε(s, χμ₂, ψ) for any μ₁μ₂ = ω_π (JL70 Proposition 3.8, proof).
(ii) follows from (iii) applied to π₁ and π₂ with the same factorisation of the common central character, and (i).
acceptance: For π = π(μ₁, μ₂) a ramified principal series and χ with c(χ) > max(c(μ₁), c(μ₂)), the twisted L-factor is 1 and ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) is the product of the two Tate constants.

Two supercuspidal representations with the same central character have equal twisted γ-factors for all sufficiently ramified χ, although they need not be isomorphic: stability alone never distinguishes them (non-example for using stability as a converse theorem).

The hypothesis on central characters is necessary in (ii): for π an unramified principal series and η an unramified character with η² ≠ 1, the highly ramified ε-factors of χ⊗(π⊗η) and χ⊗π differ by the factor η²(ϖ)^{c(χ)+n(ψ)} (n(ψ) the conductor exponent of ψ), which is not 1 for suitable large c(χ).

nodes.title: The GL₂ local converse theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a nonarchimedean local field of characteristic zero and ψ a nontrivial additive character. Let π and π′ be irreducible infinite-dimensional admissible representations of GL₂(F) with the same central character. Then π ≅ π′ if and only if γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = γ(s, χ⊗π′, ψ) for every quasi-character χ of F^×. Equivalently, without the central-character hypothesis, π ≅ π′ as soon as L(s, χ⊗π) = L(s, χ⊗π′) and ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π′, ψ) for every character χ of F^× (Bushnell–Henniart's form, which also covers one-dimensional representations). It suffices to test χ of finite order with χ(ϖ) = 1 for a fixed uniformiser ϖ: every quasi-character is such a χ times |·|^t, and twisting by |·|^t replaces s by s + t in all three factors.
hypotheses: F is a finite extension of Q_p, ψ a nontrivial additive character, ϖ a uniformiser.
π, π′ are irreducible admissible infinite-dimensional (equivalently generic, R16.2/local-classification) representations of GL₂(F) with ω_π = ω_{π′}.
γ(s, χ⊗π, ψ) = ε(s, χ⊗π, ψ)L(1−s, χ⁻¹⊗π̃)/L(s, χ⊗π) with the Jacquet–Langlands factors.
proofSteps: The implication from isomorphism to equality of factors is immediate.

Converse (JL70 Theorem 2.18 and Corollary 2.19): in the Kirillov model both representations are realised on spaces containing C_c^∞(F^×); the local functional equation of Theorem 2.18(iv) expresses the action of the Weyl element on C_c^∞(F^×) through the twisted γ-factors, by Mellin inversion over the characters of O_F^× and the variable s. Equal γ-factors and equal central characters therefore give the same action of the Borel subgroup and of the Weyl element on the common subspace, which generates; so π ≅ π′.

Reduction to finite-order twists with χ(ϖ) = 1: a quasi-character χ equals χ₀|·|^t with χ₀(ϖ) = 1 and χ₀ of finite order on O_F^× (it is continuous on a profinite group), and γ(s, χ₀|·|^t⊗π, ψ) = γ(s + t, χ₀⊗π, ψ).

Bushnell–Henniart prove the version with L and ε (27.1): by 27.2 a representation is cuspidal exactly when all its twisted L-factors are 1, so equal twisted factors separate cuspidal from non-cuspidal representations; non-cuspidal ones are then recovered from their principal-series parameters, and cuspidal ones from their types through Gauss sums (27.8).
acceptance: For π = π(μ₁, μ₂) and π′ = π(μ₁′, μ₂′) irreducible principal series with equal central characters, equal twisted γ-factors force {μ₁, μ₂} = {μ₁′, μ₂′}: twist by χ = μ₁⁻¹ and compare the zero of 1/L(s, χ⊗π) at s = 0.

For η the unramified quadratic character, π and π⊗η have the same central character and γ(s, χ⊗π⊗η, ψ) = γ(s + πi/log q, χ⊗π, ψ); the criterion says π ≅ π⊗η exactly when every twisted γ-factor is invariant under this shift of s, which holds for the supercuspidal representations induced from the unramified quadratic extension and fails for unramified principal series π(μ, ν) with {μη, νη} ≠ {μ, ν}.
A one-dimensional representation χ∘det is excluded from the γ-form (not generic), but is covered by Bushnell–Henniart's L-and-ε form.

nodes.title: A global twist with one prescribed component and high ramification elsewhere
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, S a finite set of finite places, v₀ ∈ S, χ₀ a quasi-character of F_{v₀}^×, and (m_v)_{v ∈ S∖{v₀}} nonnegative integers. There is a quasi-character ω of the idele class group C_F = F^×\A_F^× whose component at v₀ is χ₀ and whose component ω_v at each v ∈ S∖{v₀} is nontrivial on the principal units 1 + 𝔭_v^{m_v}, so that c(ω_v) > m_v. Nothing is imposed at the other places; ω has finite order on the units at every finite place but need not have finite order globally. This is Jacquet–Langlands's Lemma 12.5, which is the only global character input of the all-place upgrade; the finite-order prescription at several places (Chevalley's congruence theorem) is not needed for it.
hypotheses: F is a number field; S is a finite set of finite places; v₀ ∈ S.
χ₀: F_{v₀}^× → C^× is a continuous quasi-character; m_v ≥ 0 are integers for v ∈ S∖{v₀}.
c(·) and 1 + 𝔭_v^m are as in AL.1/local-quasicharacter-conductor.
proofSteps: Reduce to a unitary χ₀: write χ₀ = |·|^r χ₀′ with χ₀′ unitary and multiply the character obtained for χ₀′ by |·|_A^r.

Let A ⊂ A_F^× be the subgroup of ideles with component 1 outside S, component in 1 + 𝔭_v^{m_v} at v ∈ S∖{v₀}, and arbitrary component at v₀. Then F^× ∩ A = {1}, and F^×A is closed in A_F^× (on any compact set of ideles the norm is bounded above and below, and F^× is discrete) (JL70 p. 210).

Choose a unitary character of A equal to χ₀ at v₀ and nontrivial on 1 + 𝔭_v^{m_v} at each v ∈ S∖{v₀} (the principal units are nontrivial profinite groups, so such characters exist). Extend it by 1 on F^× to the closed subgroup F^×A, then to a unitary character of A_F^× by Pontryagin duality for locally compact abelian groups; it is trivial on F^× and so is a character of C_F (JL70 p. 211).
acceptance: With S = {v₀} the lemma only asks for a Hecke character with prescribed component at one place.

For F = Q, S = {p} and χ₀ unramified with χ₀(p) = −1, the unitary unramified character ω = |·|_A^{iπ/log p} is admissible; it has infinite order, so the lemma is not a statement about finite-order characters.

nodes.title: Functional equation of twisted Artin L-functions
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, ψ = ⊗ψ_v a nontrivial character of A_F/F and dx = ∏dx_v the Tamagawa measure. Let ρ: G_F → GL_n(C) be continuous (so of finite image) and ω a quasi-character of C_F, viewed as a character of W_F through global reciprocity; put V = ρ⊗ω, a representation of the global Weil group W_F. Its completed L-function Λ(s, V) = ∏_v L(s, V_v), the product over all places with the archimedean Γ-factors, converges in a half-plane Re s > σ₀, extends meromorphically to C, and satisfies Λ(s, V) = ε(s, V)Λ(1 − s, V^∨) with ε(s, V) = ∏_v ε(s, V_v, ψ_v, dx_v), the product of the Langlands–Deligne local constants (almost all equal to 1); ε(s, V) does not depend on ψ. Here V_v is the restriction to W_{F_v} and the local factors are those of R01.2 at finite places and of AL.1/AF.1 at archimedean places. No holomorphy of Λ(s, V) is asserted.
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL_n(C) is a continuous homomorphism; ω: A_F^×/F^× → C^× is a continuous quasi-character.
Global reciprocity identifies W_F^{ab} with C_F in the normalisation of R01.2/local-epsilon-factor (uniformisers to geometric Frobenius), and V = ρ⊗ω is a continuous representation of W_F.
Local constants: Deligne's ε(V_v, ψ_v, dx_v) at finite places (R01.2/local-epsilon-factor) and the archimedean constants of AL.1 and R16.3/archimedean-factor-comparison.
proofSteps: ρ factors through G = Gal(L/F) for a finite Galois L/F (R01.1/finite-galois-factorisation). By Brauer's induction theorem (Tau Ceti InductionRestriction, Layer 6) the character of ρ is an integral combination Σ nᵢ Ind_{Hᵢ}^{G} θᵢ of characters induced from linear characters θᵢ of subgroups Hᵢ = Gal(L/Kᵢ).
By the projection formula, V = ρ⊗ω is the corresponding virtual combination Σ nᵢ Ind_{W_{Kᵢ}}^{W_F}(θᵢ·(ω∘N_{Kᵢ/F})). Global reciprocity turns θᵢ·(ω∘N_{Kᵢ/F}) into a quasi-character of C_{Kᵢ}.

Local L-factors are additive and inductive (R01.2/local-factor-of-induced-representation at finite places, the Γ-factor identities of AL.1 at archimedean ones), so Λ(s, V) = ∏ᵢ Λ_{Kᵢ}(s, θᵢ ω_{Kᵢ})^{nᵢ}; each factor is a completed Hecke L-function, meromorphic with Hecke–Tate functional equation (AL.1/hecke-l-functional-equation).

Local constants are additive and inductive in degree zero (Deligne Théorème 4.1 (1)–(4)); comparing the induced permutation representations with Dedekind zeta functions shows that the product over all places of the inductivity constants λ(Kᵢ/F) is 1, so ∏_v ε(s, V_v) = ∏ᵢ ε_{Kᵢ}(s, θᵢω_{Kᵢ})^{nᵢ} (Deligne 5.11). Dividing the functional equations gives the claim; independence of ψ follows from the product formula for ε under ψ ↦ ψ(a·) with a ∈ F^×.
acceptance: For ρ trivial of dimension one the statement is Hecke–Tate's functional equation for Λ(s, ω).

For ρ = Ind_{G_K}^{G_F} 1 the left side is the completed Dedekind zeta function of K twisted by ω∘N_{K/F}; a pole occurs exactly when ω∘N_{K/F} = |·|^{iu}, and then at s = 1 − iu, showing that holomorphy is not part of the statement.
For a two-dimensional dihedral ρ = Ind θ the equation coincides with that of the Hecke L-function of θ·(ω∘N), consistent with JL70 Proposition 12.1.

sources.locator: §4, Théorème 4.1 (1)–(4), printed p. 535 (PDF p. 35)
sources.match: Existence and uniqueness of local constants that are multiplicative in exact sequences, scale with the measure, are inductive in degree zero and equal Tate's constants for characters.

For a representation of the global Weil group, the global L-function and the product of local constants satisfy the functional equation; Deligne derives it from the preceding local results and the classical arguments (Brauer induction, Hecke).

sources.match: Jacquet and Langlands use this functional equation for ω⊗σ with σ a two-dimensional Weil-group representation, with ε given by the product of local constants, in the isolation argument.

nodes.title: From weak Artin matching to matching at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, viewed on W_F, and π a cuspidal automorphic representation of GL₂(A_F). For each place v let π(ρ_v) be the irreducible generic representation of GL₂(F_v) whose arithmetic-normalised R16.3 parameter (AF.1 at archimedean v) is ρ|_{W_{F_v}}. Suppose there is a finite set T of finite places such that π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for every finite v ∉ T and for every archimedean v. Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for every place v. In particular the central character of π is det ρ (read through global reciprocity), and for every quasi-character χ of C_F and every place v the local factors agree: L(s, π_v⊗χ_v) = L(s, ρ_v⊗χ_v) and ε(s, π_v⊗χ_v, ψ_v) = ε(s, ρ_v⊗χ_v, ψ_v); in particular L(s, π⊗χ) = L(s, ρ⊗χ) for the completed L-functions, which are therefore entire when ρ is irreducible. The archimedean hypothesis cannot be dropped from this argument: it is what lets the archimedean factors cancel (Langlands's unproved Lemma 3.2 would be needed otherwise).
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous (finite image); π is cuspidal automorphic on GL₂(A_F).

π(ρ_v) is defined through the rank-two local Langlands correspondence of R16.3 (finite v) and AF.1/archimedean-llc-gln (archimedean v), with the Tate–unitary normalisation of R16.3/tate-unitary-normalization; since ρ_v has bounded image and N = 0, π(ρ_v) is tempered and generic.
T is a finite set of finite places; π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for all finite v ∉ T and all archimedean v.
proofSteps: Central characters. ω_π and det ρ (a quasi-character of C_F by reciprocity) agree at every v ∉ T, because the correspondence matches central characters with determinants. Their quotient is a Hecke character trivial on F_v^× for all v ∉ T; as F^× is dense in ∏_{v ∈ T}F_v^× (weak approximation), it is trivial. Hence ω_{π_v} = det ρ_v for every v, including v ∈ T.

Fix v₀ ∈ T and a quasi-character χ₀ of F_{v₀}^×. For each v ∈ T∖{v₀}, gl2-twist-stability applied to π_v and π(ρ_v), which have the same central character by the first step, gives a bound m_v. isolating-twist-character supplies ω on C_F with ω_{v₀} = χ₀ and c(ω_v) > m_v for v ∈ T∖{v₀}.

π⊗ω is cuspidal, so its completed L-function satisfies the functional equation of R16.5/global-epsilon-normalization with ε the product of local ε-factors (JL70 Theorem 11.1, p. 179); ρ⊗ω satisfies artin-twisted-functional-equation with the same additive character ψ. At every v ∉ T the local L- and ε-factors of π_v⊗ω_v and ρ_v⊗ω_v coincide (hypothesis and the factor compatibilities of R16.3, including R16.3/archimedean-factor-comparison at infinity). Dividing the two functional equations by the common partial L-functions gives ∏_{v ∈ T} γ(s, π_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) = ∏_{v ∈ T} γ(s, ρ_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) as meromorphic functions (JL70 p. 210).

For v ∈ T∖{v₀}, γ(s, ρ_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) = γ(s, π(ρ_v)⊗ω_v, ψ_v) by R16.3, and this equals γ(s, π_v⊗ω_v, ψ_v) by gl2-twist-stability. Cancelling leaves γ(s, π_{v₀}⊗χ₀, ψ_{v₀}) = γ(s, π(ρ_{v₀})⊗χ₀, ψ_{v₀}) for the arbitrary χ₀.

π_{v₀} is infinite-dimensional (local components of cuspidal representations are generic: R16.4/global-whittaker-expansion), as is π(ρ_{v₀}); their central characters agree; gl2-local-converse gives π_{v₀} ≅ π(ρ_{v₀}). The factor identities follow from R16.3; the global identity follows, and for irreducible ρ the twisted L-functions are entire because L(s, π⊗χ) is the standard L-function of a cuspidal representation of GL₂ (AL.2/global-godement-jacquet).
acceptance: For a dihedral ρ = Ind_{G_K}^{G_F} θ the conclusion recovers the all-place local components of quadratic automorphic induction (JL70 Proposition 12.1), where T can be taken empty.
With T = {v₀} the stability step is vacuous and the conclusion is the local converse theorem applied to the single quotient of functional equations.

nodes.title: Tetrahedral Artin automorphy at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, irreducible, with projective image A₄, and let π be the cuspidal representation of R17.5/tetrahedral-artin (the cubic descent of the dihedral π(ρ_E), with ω_π = det ρ). Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place v of F, including the archimedean ones and the places dividing 2 where ρ_v may be primitive. In particular all twisted L- and ε-factors of π and ρ agree at every place. At an archimedean v the component is π(1, 1) if ρ(c_v) = 1, π(sgn, sgn) if ρ(c_v) = −1 and the weight-one limit π(1, sgn) if ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution; at a complex v it is π(1, 1).
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous and irreducible with projective image A₄.
E/F is the cyclic cubic extension cut out by the preimage of the normal subgroup V₄ ⊂ A₄; P = ρ|_{W_E} is dihedral, and π(P) is its quadratic automorphic induction (R17.5/dihedral-artin).
π is the cyclic descent of π(P) to F with ω_π = det ρ constructed in R17.5/tetrahedral-artin; it satisfies π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for almost all v.
proofSteps: Archimedean places. Every archimedean v of F splits completely in E: the decomposition group at v has order at most 2 inside Gal(E/F) ≅ Z/3. For w | v, E_w = F_v, and R17.4/cyclic-base-change gives BC_{E/F}(π)_w ≅ π_v at the split place. By construction BC_{E/F}(π) ≅ π(P) (R17.4/cyclic-descent), and π(P)_w ≅ π(P_w) at every place by quadratic induction (R17.5/quadratic-induction, JL70 Proposition 12.1). As P_w = ρ|_{W_{E_w}} = ρ_v, π_v ≅ π(ρ_v).

The explicit archimedean components: ρ(W_C) is trivial (a connected group maps trivially to the profinite G_F), so ρ_v is a sum of characters of W_R/C^× ≅ {±1} determined by ρ(c_v), and AF.1/archimedean-llc-gln gives the listed principal series.
Finite places. R17.5/tetrahedral-artin gives π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) outside a finite set T of finite places. artin-all-place-upgrade, with the archimedean matching just proved, extends this to every place.
acceptance: If the image of ρ is the binary tetrahedral group, whose only involution is −1, then ρ(c_v) is scalar at every real v and π_v is π(1, 1) or π(sgn, sgn); an odd tetrahedral ρ over Q (det ρ(c) = −1) has a non-scalar involution in its image and π_∞ is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn).

At an unramified place inert in E, R17.5/tetrahedral-artin removes a cube-root-of-unity ambiguity in the Satake class by a group-theoretic argument; at the finitely many places that argument does not reach (places ramified for ρ, in particular those over 2 where ρ_v can be primitive) only artin-all-place-upgrade identifies π_v.

Replacing π by π⊗η with η the cubic character of E/F gives a representation with the same base change to E but different central character; it is not π(ρ), so the determinant normalisation of R17.5/tetrahedral-artin is essential.

nodes.title: Octahedral Artin automorphy at every place
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field and ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) continuous, irreducible, with projective image S₄, and let π be the cuspidal representation of R17.5/octahedral-artin (Tunnell's choice among the two quadratic descents of the tetrahedral representation of ρ|_{G_E}, E/F the quadratic field of the preimage of A₄). Then π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place v of F. At a real place v that is complex in E, ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution (its projective image is a transposition), ρ_v = 1⊕sgn and π_v is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn); at real places split in E and at complex places the component is read off from the tetrahedral representation over E.
hypotheses: F is a number field; ρ: G_F → GL₂(C) is continuous and irreducible with projective image S₄.
E/F is the quadratic extension cut out by the preimage of A₄; ρ_E = ρ|_{G_E} has projective image A₄; π_E is its tetrahedral cuspidal representation (tetrahedral-artin-all-places over E).
π is the quadratic descent of π_E singled out by Tunnell's lemma in R17.5/octahedral-artin, with π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) for almost all v.
proofSteps: Central character. As in artin-all-place-upgrade, ω_π = det ρ, since both agree at almost all places.

Archimedean v split in E, and complex v: for w | v, E_w = F_v and BC_{E/F}(π)_w ≅ π_v (R17.4/cyclic-base-change); BC_{E/F}(π) ≅ π_E because π is a quadratic descent of π_E, which matches ρ_E at every place of E by tetrahedral-artin-all-places applied over E; so π_v ≅ π(ρ_v).

Real v with E_w = C: ρ(c_v) lies outside the preimage of A₄, so its projective image is an odd involution of S₄, a transposition; hence ρ(c_v) is a non-scalar involution, det ρ(c_v) = −1 and ρ_v = 1⊕sgn. By R17.4/local-compatibility the parameter φ of π_v restricts to W_C as the parameter of BC_{E/F}(π)_w = π_{E,w} = π(1, 1), so φ is trivial on C^× and φ ∈ {1⊕1, 1⊕sgn, sgn⊕sgn}. Its determinant is ω_{π_v} = det ρ_v, which is sgn; only 1⊕sgn has determinant sgn, so π_v ≅ π(1, sgn) = π(ρ_v).
Finite places: artin-all-place-upgrade with the archimedean matching just proved.
acceptance: For F = Q and ρ = s∘r̄ with r̄: G_Q → GL₂(F₃) odd and surjective (R17.5/octahedral-mod-three-application), E is the quadratic field cut out by det r̄, which is imaginary because det r̄(c) = −1; the real place is complex in E and π_∞ is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn).

The two descents π₁ and π₂ = π₁⊗ω_{E/F} have the same central character and the same base change to E; at a real place complex in E they have the same archimedean component as well (twisting by ω_{E/F} sends π(1, sgn) to π(sgn, 1) ≅ π(1, sgn)), so archimedean matching does not choose between them: Tunnell's cubic comparison does.
The archimedean step uses only the quadratic descent and the central character; Tunnell's cubic comparison and the upgrade are still needed at the finite places.

nodes.title: The Brauer character of a modular representation
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a finite group, p a prime, k an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, m ≥ 1 an integer prime to p that is divisible by the order of every p-regular element of Γ (for instance the prime-to-p part of the exponent of Γ), and τ: μ_m(k) → μ_m(C) a group isomorphism. For a representation r: Γ → GL_n(k) and a p-regular g ∈ Γ (order prime to p), r(g) is diagonalisable and its eigenvalues λ₁, …, λ_n, counted with algebraic multiplicity, lie in μ_m(k). The Brauer character of r is the complex-valued function on the p-regular elements φ_r(g) = τ(λ₁) + … + τ(λ_n). It depends on τ, is defined only on p-regular elements, and is not a lift of the trace of r(g) ∈ k (Webb's Example 10.1.2 has trace 1 and Brauer character −1). For a representation over a subfield k₀ ⊂ k (for example a finite field) one takes the Brauer character of its extension of scalars to k.
hypotheses: Γ is a finite group and p is prime; k is algebraically closed of characteristic p.
m is prime to p and divisible by the order of every p-regular element of Γ; τ: μ_m(k) ≅ μ_m(C) is an isomorphism of cyclic groups of order m.
r: Γ → GL_n(k) is a group homomorphism (equivalently a finite-dimensional kΓ-module with a basis); φ_r is defined on {g ∈ Γ : gcd(ord g, p) = 1}.
proofSteps: For g p-regular, r(g)^{ord g} = 1 and ord g is prime to p, so X^{ord g} − 1 is separable over k; r(g) is diagonalisable with eigenvalues in μ_{ord g}(k) ⊂ μ_m(k) (Webb §10.1, before Example 10.1.2).
Define φ_r(g) as the sum of τ over the roots of the characteristic polynomial of r(g), with multiplicity; this is independent of any ordering and of the basis.

For a p-modular system (F, R, k) with F of characteristic zero containing μ_m, reduction modulo the maximal ideal is an isomorphism μ_m(R) → μ_m(k) (Webb Lemma 10.1.1; R01.1/reduction-of-roots-of-unity proves it for the algebraic closure of Q_p); choosing τ as the composite of its inverse with an embedding F → C makes the Brauer character of a reduced lattice equal to the ordinary character (API brauerCharacter_reduction).
acceptance: The listed tests hold, and the API items listed above are consistent with Webb Proposition 10.1.3 (1)–(6).
brauerCharacter agrees with the ordinary character of any integral lift on p-regular elements, which is the property used by brauer-character-recognition and fong-swan.

nodes.title: Brauer characters determine composition factors
nodes.statement: Let Γ be finite, k algebraically closed of characteristic p, and φ the Brauer character for a fixed τ. (a) The Brauer characters of the simple kΓ-modules S₁, …, S_r are linearly independent over C and form a basis of the class functions on p-regular conjugacy classes; the Brauer characters of their projective covers P_{S₁}, …, P_{S_r} form the dual basis for the pairing ⟨α, β⟩ = |Γ|⁻¹ Σ_{g p-regular} α(g⁻¹)β(g), with ⟨φ_{P_{S_i}}, φ_{S_j}⟩ = δ_{ij}. (b) Two finite-dimensional kΓ-modules have the same Brauer character if and only if they have the same composition factors with the same multiplicities; in particular a module whose Brauer character equals that of a simple module S is isomorphic to S. (c) Let (F, R, k₀) be a p-modular system with F of characteristic zero containing the m-th roots of unity, uniformiser ϖ, k₀ ⊂ k, and τ compatible with reduction of roots of unity and an embedding F → C. For a full RΓ-lattice L in an FΓ-module V, the Brauer character of (L/ϖL) ⊗_{k₀} k is the ordinary character of V restricted to p-regular elements; different full lattices give reductions with the same composition factors (Brauer–Nesbitt).
hypotheses: Γ finite; k algebraically closed of characteristic p (a splitting field for Γ); τ as in R17.5/brauer-character.

In (c): R is a discrete valuation ring with uniformiser ϖ, fraction field F of characteristic zero containing μ_m, and residue field k₀ ⊂ k; τ(ζ mod ϖ) = σ(ζ) for ζ ∈ μ_m(R) and a fixed embedding σ: F → C.
proofSteps: (c) For p-regular g, the eigenvalues of g on V lie in μ_m(F) ⊂ R and reduce to the eigenvalues on L/ϖL, so the two sums agree under τ (Webb Proposition 10.1.3(6) with Lemma 10.1.1). Brauer–Nesbitt for lattices (Webb Theorem 9.4.8; R01.1/brauer-nesbitt for the characteristic-polynomial form) gives the independence of the lattice.

(a) Each P_{S_i} has S_i as unique simple quotient, so dim Hom_{kΓ}(P_{S_i}, S_j) = δ_{ij} since k is a splitting field; this Hom dimension is computed by the pairing of Brauer characters (Webb Proposition 10.2.1, p. 174). The number of simple modules equals the number of p-regular classes (Brauer), so the two families are dual bases (Webb Theorem 10.2.2). Projective covers of finite-dimensional algebras and the Cartan map come from Tau Ceti's GrothendieckEulerForms, Layer 4.

(b) Brauer characters are additive in short exact sequences (R17.5/brauer-character, API brauerCharacter_blockTriangular), so φ_U = Σ_S [U : S] φ_S; by (a) the multiplicities [U : S] are determined by φ_U (Webb Corollary 10.2.3(3)). If φ_U = φ_S for simple S, U has a single composition factor S and so U ≅ S.
acceptance: Webb's Example 10.1.2: the two-dimensional F₂C₃-module U (simple over F₂) becomes, over k, the sum of the two nontrivial characters; its Brauer character at the generator is −1, while two trivial factors give 2 and a trivial plus a nontrivial factor give 1 + ζ with ζ a primitive cube root of unity, so the composition factors are read off from the value.

In characteristic p, the regular representation of a cyclic p-group has the same Brauer character (|Γ| at 1) as |Γ| copies of the trivial module but is not semisimple: (b) determines composition factors, not the module.
(c) for Γ of order prime to p recovers the bijection between simple modules in characteristic zero and in characteristic p (Webb Theorem 9.4.11, p. 155).

nodes.title: The Fong–Swan theorem
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a finite p-solvable group (in particular any finite solvable group), k an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, and τ as in R17.5/brauer-character. Every irreducible Brauer character φ of Γ is the restriction to p-regular elements of an irreducible ordinary character: there is a complex irreducible representation with character χ such that χ(g) = φ(g) for every p-regular g. Equivalently (module form): for any splitting p-modular system (F, R, k₀) for Γ, every simple k₀Γ-module is the reduction modulo π of an RΓ-lattice. Isaacs's proof gives a p-rational χ (values in a cyclotomic field of conductor prime to p); for p odd this p-rational lift is unique. The theorem fails for groups that are not p-solvable (it is a property of p-solvable groups, not of all finite groups).
hypotheses: Γ is finite and p-solvable: it has a normal series whose factors are p-groups or p′-groups; finite solvable groups qualify.
k is algebraically closed of characteristic p; Brauer characters are taken with respect to τ.
Module form: (F, R, k₀) is a p-modular system in which F and k₀ are splitting fields for Γ (Webb §9.4).
proofSteps: Character form, by induction on |Γ| (Isaacs Theorem 5.4). Case 1: some characteristic subgroup N has a number of distinct irreducible Brauer constituents of φ_N divisible by p. For such a constituent μ the inertia group T is proper; Clifford theory for Brauer characters (Isaacs Lemma 5.1) gives ϑ ∈ IBr(T) whose induced Brauer character is φ; the induction hypothesis lifts ϑ to an ordinary character η of T, and the character induced from η is an irreducible lift of φ.

Case 2: no such N. For a proper characteristic M and a constituent μ of φ_M, induction gives a p-rational lift θ of μ with p ∤ θ(1), whose number of Γ-conjugates is prime to p. If O^p(Γ) is proper, take M = O^p(Γ): θ is Γ-invariant, Gallagher's theorem (Isaacs Theorem 4.2) extends it uniquely to χ with p ∤ o(χ), and Isaacs Lemma 4.1 gives χ* = φ. If O^p(Γ) = Γ, then M = O^{p′}(Γ) is proper with Γ/M a p′-group, and Isaacs Theorem 3.1 gives a unique constituent χ of the induced character of θ with χ* = φ. p-solvability guarantees that one of O^p(Γ), O^{p′}(Γ) is proper.

Module form from the character form: realise χ over F (a splitting field), take a full RΓ-lattice L in the realisation (Webb Corollary 9.4.7: span of the Γ-translates of a basis); by brauer-character-recognition (c) the Brauer character of L/πL is χ* = φ, and by (b) L/πL ≅ S.
acceptance: The two-dimensional simple module of S₃ in characteristic 2 lifts to the reflection representation of S₃, although 2 divides |S₃|.
For Γ of order prime to p the theorem is the classical bijection between simple modules in characteristic zero and characteristic p (Webb Theorem 9.4.11, p. 155), and every lift is unique.

For a cyclic p-group the only irreducible Brauer character is trivial, and its lifts are all p-power-order characters; for p odd the p-rational one is the trivial character, illustrating Isaacs's uniqueness.
p-solvability cannot be dropped: A₅ ≅ SL₂(F₄) has a two-dimensional irreducible Brauer character at p = 2 (its natural representation), but no irreducible complex character of degree 2.

nodes.title: Integral lifts of representations of finite solvable groups
nodes.statement: Let p be prime, Γ a finite solvable group, k an algebraically closed field of characteristic p and r: Γ → GL_n(k) an irreducible representation. There exist a number field E, a height-one prime λ of O_E above p, the localisation R = (O_E)_λ (a discrete valuation ring), a ring homomorphism f: R → k with kernel λR, a group homomorphism ρ: Γ → GL_n(R) and P ∈ GL_n(k) such that r(g) = P·f(ρ(g))·P⁻¹ for every g ∈ Γ. One may take E to contain the e-th roots of unity, e the exponent of Γ. If r is injective so is ρ, and in general ker ρ = ker r. The reduction is isomorphic to r itself, not only after semisimplification; neither p ∤ |Γ| nor n = 2 is assumed.
hypotheses: p is prime; Γ is a finite solvable group; k is algebraically closed of characteristic p.
r: Γ → GL_n(k) is a homomorphism whose representation on kⁿ is irreducible (equivalently absolutely irreducible, as k is algebraically closed).
proofSteps: Descend r to a finite field: its finitely many matrix entries generate a finite subfield k₀ ⊂ k (R01.1/residual-descent-to-a-finite-field); enlarge k₀ = F_q so that it contains the prime-to-p roots of unity of order dividing e, making it a splitting field for Γ in characteristic p (Brauer; Webb Theorem 9.2.7, read with the prime-to-p part of e, see E18). The k₀Γ-module S₀ = k₀ⁿ is simple and S₀ ⊗ k ≅ r.

Take E = Q(ζ_{e(q−1)}) and λ a prime above p. E contains μ_e, so it is a splitting field for Γ in characteristic zero (Webb Theorem 9.2.7); the residue field κ(λ) contains F_p(ζ_{q−1}) = F_q, and contains the unique copy of k₀. R = (O_E)_λ is a discrete valuation ring, so (E, R, κ(λ)) is a splitting p-modular system.

fong-swan (module form) gives an RΓ-lattice L with L/λL ≅ S₀ ⊗_{k₀} κ(λ). L is finitely generated and torsion-free over the discrete valuation ring R, hence free of rank n (Webb Lemma 9.4.6, Corollary 9.4.7); a basis gives ρ: Γ → GL_n(R).

Choose f: R → κ(λ) → k extending the given inclusion k₀ ⊂ k (possible since k is algebraically closed and κ(λ) is a finite extension of k₀). Then f∘ρ ≅ S₀ ⊗ k ≅ r, which gives P. If ρ(g) = 1 then r(g) = P·P⁻¹ = 1, so ker ρ ⊂ ker r. Running the construction for the faithful representation of the solvable quotient Γ/ker r and composing with the quotient map gives ρ with ker ρ = ker r; in particular ρ is injective when r is.
acceptance: Γ = S₃, p = 2, r the two-dimensional simple module: the lift is the reflection representation over Z[ζ₃] localised at 2, whose reduction is r.
Γ = GL₂(F₃), p = 3, r the identity representation over F₃ ⊂ F̄₃: a lift is the section into GL₂(Z[√−2]) of R17.5/octahedral-mod-three-application, with λ = (1 + √−2).
For Γ of order prime to p and n = 1 the lift is the Teichmüller lift of a character (R01.1/teichmuller-lift-of-a-residual-character).
Changing the basis of L changes P; entrywise equality r(g) = f(ρ(g)) is not part of the statement.

nodes.title: Reduction at an odd prime detects the determinant of an involution
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring without zero divisors, k a field in which 2 ≠ 0, f: R → k a ring homomorphism and A ∈ GL₂(R) with A² = 1. If det f(A) = −1 then det A = −1. The same holds if only B = P·f(A)·P⁻¹ with det B = −1 is known, for some P ∈ GL₂(k). Consequently, for a homomorphism ρ: G → GL₂(R), an element c ∈ G with c² = 1 and a residual representation r̄ = P·(f∘ρ)·P⁻¹ with det r̄(c) = −1, one has det ρ(c) = −1. The hypothesis 2 ≠ 0 in k is necessary: in characteristic 2 the identity matrix has residual determinant 1 = −1 but integral determinant 1.
hypotheses: R is a commutative ring with no zero divisors; k is a field with 2 ≠ 0; f: R → k is a ring homomorphism.
A ∈ GL₂(R) satisfies A² = 1; P ∈ GL₂(k).
proofSteps: det(A)² = det(A²) = 1, so det A = ±1 in the domain R.
If det A = 1 then det f(A) = f(1) = 1, and 1 = −1 in k would force 2 = 0; hence det A = −1.
Conjugation by P does not change the determinant, which gives the residual-conjugacy form and the statement for ρ(c).
acceptance: Over Z, diag(1, −1) reduced modulo 3 is odd, and the lemma recovers that its determinant is −1.
The scalar matrix −I has determinant +1 in rank two, so a scalar involution is never odd.
Modulo 2 the identity matrix has residual determinant −1 = 1 while its determinant over Z is 1: the lemma fails without 2 ≠ 0.

nodes.title: Characteristic-zero lifts of residual representations with solvable image
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, p a prime, k = F̄_p (or any algebraically closed field of characteristic p, with the discrete topology) and r̄: G_F → GL_n(k) a continuous absolutely irreducible representation whose image is solvable. There exist a number field E, a prime λ of E above p, R = (O_E)_λ, f: R → k with kernel λR, a homomorphism ρ: G_F → GL_n(R) with open kernel (so continuous for the discrete and for the λ-adic topology on GL_n(R)) and P ∈ GL_n(k) with r̄(g) = P·f(ρ(g))·P⁻¹ for all g ∈ G_F, such that: ker ρ = ker r̄ (so ρ has finite image isomorphic to that of r̄, cuts out the same field, and is unramified at every place where r̄ is); for every embedding E → C, ρ is irreducible over C; its image, and so its projective image, is solvable. If n = 2, p > 2 and r̄ is totally odd (det r̄(c_v) = −1 for every complex conjugation c_v at a real place v), then ρ is totally odd. This strengthens R17.5/odd-residual-lift: the reduction is r̄ itself, not only its semisimplification; F need not be totally real for the lifting part; and no projective lifting, Tate vanishing or Teichmüller twist is used. For p = 2 the oddness clause fails; the characteristic-two case is planned in layer R17.6 of this roadmap.
hypotheses: F is a number field; p is prime; k is algebraically closed of characteristic p, with the discrete topology.
r̄: G_F → GL_n(k) is continuous, absolutely irreducible, and r̄(G_F) is a solvable group.
Oddness clause: n = 2, p > 2, and det r̄(c_v) = −1 for the complex conjugations c_v at all real places v.
proofSteps: Continuity with discrete coefficients means ker r̄ is open and Γ = r̄(G_F) is finite (R01.1/finite-coefficients-and-finite-quotients).

Apply solvable-integral-lift to the inclusion Γ ⊂ GL_n(k), irreducible because r̄ is: this gives E, λ, R, f, an injective ρ_Γ: Γ → GL_n(R) and P. Put ρ = ρ_Γ ∘ r̄; then ker ρ = ker r̄ is open, so ρ is continuous, and r̄ = P·(f∘ρ)·P⁻¹.

Irreducibility over C: if ρ ⊗ C had a proper invariant subspace W, its character would be χ_W + χ_{W′} with both summands characters of nonzero representations; realising them over a finite extension of E and reducing lattices, brauer-character-recognition (c) would give r̄ at least two composition factors, contradicting (b) and the simplicity of r̄.
Oddness: for each real v, c_v² = 1; involution-oddness-under-reduction with the residual comparison P gives det ρ(c_v) = −1.
acceptance: For p = 3 and r̄: G_Q → GL₂(F₃) surjective and odd, one admissible lift is s∘r̄ with the section s of R17.5/octahedral-mod-three-application; the theorem produces some lift with the same kernel, not necessarily that one.
For p = 2 and r̄ with dihedral image the lifting part holds but the oddness clause does not: every characteristic-two residual representation has det r̄(c) = 1 = −1.
A residual representation with nonsolvable image, for example r̄ onto GL₂(F₅) ⊃ SL₂(F₅), is outside the statement; its finite lifts need not exist with the same kernel.

nodes.title: Residual representations with solvable image are automorphic of weight one
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, p an odd prime and r̄: G_F → GL₂(F̄_p) continuous and absolutely irreducible with solvable image, and let ρ, λ, f, P be the lift of R17.5/odd-solvable-residual-lift. There is a unique cuspidal automorphic representation π of GL₂(A_F) with π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place v; it is unramified at every finite place where r̄ is unramified, its central character is det ρ, and the reduction of ρ along the lattice R² is r̄ (after conjugation by P). If F is totally real and r̄ is totally odd, then π is holomorphic of parallel weight one in Rogawski–Tunnell's sense: π_v is the weight-one limit π(1, sgn) at every real place. This is the residual modularity input of the solvable case of Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Pilloni, Proposition 10.1.3; it is R17.5/residual-lt-application with its lifting step proved. No statement about the level, ordinarity or a weight-two form is made here.
hypotheses: F is a number field; p is an odd prime.
r̄: G_F → GL₂(F̄_p) is continuous, absolutely irreducible, with solvable image; ρ, E, λ, R, f, P are as produced by odd-solvable-residual-lift.
Weight-one clause: F totally real and det r̄(c_v) = −1 at every real place v; 'holomorphic of parallel weight one' is Rogawski–Tunnell's definition (R17.5/tr-weight-one).
proofSteps: ρ is irreducible with finite solvable image (odd-solvable-residual-lift), so R17.5/solvable-artin gives a cuspidal π matching ρ: in the dihedral case at every place (R17.5/dihedral-artin), in the tetrahedral and octahedral cases at every place by tetrahedral-artin-all-places and octahedral-artin-all-places. Uniqueness is strong multiplicity one (R16.4/strong-multiplicity-one).
Since ker ρ = ker r̄, ρ_v is unramified wherever r̄ is, so π_v is an unramified principal series there (R16.3/principal-series-parameter).
Weight one: at a real v, ρ(c_v) is an involution with det ρ(c_v) = −1 (oddness clause), hence non-scalar, ρ_v = 1⊕sgn and π_v ≅ π(1, sgn), which is Rogawski–Tunnell's π₁ (R17.5/tr-weight-one).
acceptance: In BCGP's situation (p = 3 or 5, F a totally real quadratic extension of the base field, r̄ = ϱ with determinant the inverse cyclotomic character, solvable image), the output is a parallel weight one cuspidal π with r̄ as residual representation; their subsequent passage to an ordinary weight-two form, which they take from Barnet-Lamb–Gee–Geraghty, is a separate input not supplied here.
If r̄ is even at some real place, the construction still gives π but its component there is π(1, 1) or π(sgn, sgn), not of weight one.
For p = 2 the theorem is not stated: the oddness clause fails, and the characteristic-two case is planned in layer R17.6 of this roadmap.

nodes.title: Odd residual representations of G_Q with solvable image come from weight-one newforms
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and r̄: G_Q → GL₂(F̄_p) continuous, irreducible and odd (det r̄(c) = −1), with solvable image. Let ρ, λ, f, P be the lift of R17.5/odd-solvable-residual-lift (n = 2, F = Q). Then there is a normalised cuspidal newform g of weight one, level N = the Artin conductor of ρ and nebentypus det ρ (an odd Dirichlet character under reciprocity), with Galois representation ρ_g ≅ ρ; consequently the reduction of ρ_g along the lattice R² is isomorphic to r̄, and for every prime ℓ ∤ N, f(a_ℓ(g)) = tr r̄(Frob_ℓ) and f(det ρ(Frob_ℓ)) = det r̄(Frob_ℓ) (arithmetic Frobenius). The prime divisors of N are exactly the primes at which r̄ is ramified, p included when r̄ is ramified at p. This is Dieulefait–Pacetti's Theorem 1.3 (Langlands–Tunnell in odd characteristic), with the lifting step written out; N can exceed Serre's conductor of r̄, and no weight-two form is constructed here.
hypotheses: p is an odd prime; r̄: G_Q → GL₂(F̄_p) is continuous and irreducible (hence absolutely irreducible, F̄_p being algebraically closed), odd, with solvable image.
Frobenius elements are arithmetic, as in Deligne–Serre; det ρ is read as a Dirichlet character by class field theory.
proofSteps: odd-solvable-residual-lift gives ρ: G_Q → GL₂(R) ⊂ GL₂(C), irreducible, odd, with finite solvable image and ker ρ = ker r̄.
R17.5/solvable-artin with tetrahedral-artin-all-places and octahedral-artin-all-places gives a cuspidal π with π_v ≅ π(ρ_v) at every place; π_∞ is the weight-one limit because ρ is odd.

R17.5/q-weight-one (Weil–Langlands, Deligne–Serre Théorème 4.10) and R16.6/weight-one-classical-comparison give the normalised weight-one newform g of level N(ρ) and nebentypus det ρ with ρ_g ≅ ρ (Deligne–Serre Théorème 4.1 for the attached representation).

Reduction: ρ_g ≅ ρ and r̄ = P·(f∘ρ)·P⁻¹ give the trace and determinant congruences; as r̄ is absolutely irreducible, every stable lattice of ρ_g has reduction isomorphic to r̄ (R01.1/brauer-nesbitt). Ramification: ker ρ = ker r̄, and the Artin conductor exponent at ℓ is positive exactly when ρ is ramified at ℓ.
acceptance: For p = 3 and r̄ surjective onto GL₂(F₃), the theorem specialises to R17.5/octahedral-mod-three-application with some lift, not necessarily the section s used there.
For a dihedral r̄ induced from a character of an imaginary quadratic field, g is a theta series of that field.
An even r̄ (det r̄(c) = 1) is excluded: its lifts are even and do not come from holomorphic weight-one forms.

sourceIssues.printed: In the solvable case the proof obtains a totally odd lift to characteristic zero with finite solvable image of the representation ϱ of G_E (E a totally real quadratic extension of the base field), using only the list of finite subgroups of GL₂ over finite fields and Tate's projective lifting theorem (their reference Ser77, Theorem 4), and then invokes Langlands and Tunnell.
sourceIssues.correction: Tate's theorem lifts a projective representation into PGL₂(C) to GL₂(C) but says nothing about reduction modulo a prime above p; the argument needs a lift whose reduction is ϱ itself. The Fong–Swan theorem for the finite solvable image of ϱ provides such a lift over the localisation of a number field at a prime above p, with the same kernel as ϱ, and total oddness follows because p > 2 (R17.5/solvable-integral-lift, R17.5/odd-solvable-residual-lift).
sourceIssues.reason: Reduction of the Tate lift is defined only after embedding the finite projective image into PGL₂ of a p-adic ring compatibly with reduction, which the proof does not construct; for p dividing the order of the image (p = 3 with image A₄ or S₄, the case of the proposition with p = 3) no prime-to-p averaging argument is available. The conclusion of the proposition is correct.
